title: the Yaksha's questions
hook: the questions turn from riddles to friends: who stands by the traveler, the householder, the sick and the dying

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Yaksha's questions began: heavier than the earth, a mother; faster than the wind, the mind. Your line was weight becomes a mother's claim. Did you look twice before reacting? Day eight hundred four.
screen: `THE YAKSHA'S QUESTIONS.` · `HEAVIER THAN THE EARTH? A MOTHER.`

segments.voice: What sleeps with its eyes open? The yaksha keeps going, and some of the questions are pure fun. Yudhishthira answers: a fish. What doesn't move once it's born? An egg. What has no heart? A stone. What grows by its own force? A river. Four brothers lie dead on the shore, and the conversation sounds almost like a game by a campfire. But listen to where it goes next. The yaksha is still asking, and Yudhishthira is still answering, one plain word at a time.
screen: `WHAT SLEEPS WITH ITS EYES OPEN?` → `A FISH, AN EGG, A STONE, A RIVER.` → `THEN, WHO STANDS BY US?`

segments.voice: Who is the friend of a traveler far from home? the yaksha asks. Yudhishthira answers: a companion on the road. Who is the friend of someone who keeps a home? The wife. Who is the friend of someone who is sick? The physician. And who is the friend of someone about to die? Charity, the gifts they've given. Four friends for four seasons of a life. It's an unglamorous list. No heroes, no gods, no armies. Just a person beside you on the road, the one you share a house with, the healer at the bedside, and at the very end, what you gave away. Remember who is answering. Yudhishthira is in exile himself, far from home, a long way from any kingdom. His companions on the road are lying dead behind him. The answer about the traveler isn't abstract for him. Then the yaksha asks about letting go. What, if you give it up, makes you agreeable? Pride, Yudhishthira says. What, given up, leaves no regret? Anger. What makes you rich, once you let it go? Desire. And what makes you happy, once it's gone? Greed. Notice how practical these are. The yaksha isn't asking about heaven yet. He's asking how to be good company, and how not to be miserable. The epic sets these answers in the mouth of a man whose brothers' lives depend on getting them right, and they come out plain and small, the kind of thing you could live by on an ordinary day.
screen: `A COMPANION FOR THE TRAVELER.` · `A HEALER FOR THE SICK.` · `CHARITY FOR THE DYING.` · then, large: `GIVE UP PRIDE, ANGER, DESIRE, GREED.`

segments.voice: Settle, and let the breath find its pace. Bring to mind, one at a time, the friends of your own seasons. Someone who was a companion when you were far from home. Someone who shares, or shared, your home. Someone who looked after you when you were sick. Let each face come and stay for a few breaths. Breathe in, and remember them. Breathe out, and thank them silently. If you pray, you can hold each one in your prayer. The bell holds the time.

Mitra, a friend, is what the yaksha asks about: for a traveler, a wife, the sick and the dying. A fish that sleeps with open eyes, four friends for four seasons, and four things worth letting go. Today's word.
Your line: a companion on the road. Today, send a word of thanks to one person who was your companion when you were far from home. Day eight hundred four.

howItsDone: The middle of the Yaksha's questions mixes riddles about fish and rivers with plain guidance: who our friends are in each season, and what is worth giving up.

match.prompt: the friends of every season — tap the pairs.

myth: Yudhishthira said the friend of the dying is the gods
he said charity: the gifts a person has given.
giving up desire, he said, makes a person rich
and giving up greed makes a person happy.
all of the yaksha's questions were serious
some were riddles: a fish sleeps with open eyes, an egg doesn't move once born.

fork.setup: you're Yudhishthira. the yaksha asks: what, if you give it up, leaves no regret? what do you answer?
fork.reveal: anger. and alongside it: give up pride and you're agreeable, desire and you're rich, greed and you're happy.

original.note: Sanskrit: mitra, a friend; the yaksha asks who is the friend of each kind of person.

trapdoor: what you thought: riddles about fish and rivers.
what it means: the questions turn to who stands by us, and what we're better off without.
what a scholar hears: the answer for the traveler, a companion, comes from a man in exile whose companions lie dead behind him.

sources.ref: Mahabharata, Vana Parva (Aranyaka Parva), the episode of the Yaksha's questions: the riddles (fish, egg, stone, river); the friend of the exile, householder, sick and dying; what is renounced (pride, anger, desire, greed)

notes: All paraphrase. Confirm in Ganguli: a fish does not close its eyes while asleep; an egg does not move after birth; a stone is without heart; a river grows (swells) by its own force.

Confirm the four friends: the friend of the exile (or traveler in a distant land) is the companion; of the householder, the wife; of the sick, the physician; of one about to die, charity. 'Wife' kept as in the text; a Keeper may want a gloss for listeners.
Confirm: pride renounced makes one agreeable; wrath renounced leaves no regret; desire renounced makes one wealthy; avarice renounced makes one happy.
The order of questions in the script is condensed; in Ganguli these sit among many others.
Editor pass: cut the templated 'Today, ...' hook closer; 'ordinary Tuesday' became 'ordinary day'; howItsDone no longer makes a claim about teachers.
Audit: riddles, the four friends and the four renunciations match Ganguli's answers. No changes needed.
